title: Ampera Energia Analytics — Curtailment losses in R$, per plant

slides.title: Curtailment losses in R$, per plant
slides.subtitle: One trusted plant ID · Ampera Energia Analytics on Databricks

notes.purpose: Set the frame: one business question (what did curtailment cost, per plant) answered on one platform.
notes.talk_track: This is a working prototype on Ampera's public data. In 24 months, R$ 8.4 bi of wind and solar output was cut by the grid operator. We can now say which plant lost how much, in R$, from data Ampera already owns.
notes.transition: Let me start with the outcome, then show how we got there.
notes.likely_question: Is this real data? Yes: public ONS, ANEEL SIGA, CCEE, Open-Meteo and INMET data. Ampera itself is fictional.

notes.purpose: Give the Diretor Comercial the four results before any architecture.
notes.talk_track: Four outcomes. One plant ID across two registries that don't join. Curtailment valued in R$ per plant. A model that beats the grid operator's own estimate on months it never saw. And answers in plain Portuguese on the same numbers. Why now: ONS has been curtailing wind and solar at scale in the Northeast in 2025–26, and owners only see it as vague lost generation.
notes.transition: Why was this hard? Because of the people asking.
notes.likely_question: How sure is the R$ 8.4 bi? It is a lower bound; slide 6 explains why.

slides.title: Two blockers, one root cause
columns: “My clients ask what curtailment cost them. I answer with a range and a caveat. I can't put a price on that, and it won't get a renewal signed.”
Head of Data & Analytics · time-to-launch, tickets
“ONS and SIGA don't join. Every new product starts with weeks of manual matching, and every client question becomes a ticket.”

notes.purpose: Name both buyers, the metric each is paid on, and tie their pain to one root cause.
notes.talk_track: The Diretor Comercial is measured on data-product revenue and renewals, and can't put a price on curtailment. The Head of Data & Analytics is measured on time-to-launch and the ticket backlog, and can't join the sources: CEG formats differ, ONS mixes plants with wind/solar complexes and state totals, and some plants have no CEG at all. Both problems come from the same place: no trusted plant ID.

notes.likely_question: Why not just join on CEG? Formats differ, complexes aggregate several plants, and some rows have no CEG.

notes.purpose: Quantify before vs after on the KPIs each buyer is measured on.
notes.talk_track: Plant-level generation now carries a unique plant ID for 99.97% of energy, and monthly totals tie to the published ONS total within 2%. Curtailment splits into wind, R$ 5.7 bi or 16.5% of expected output, and solar, R$ 2.6 bi or 28.2%. The AI step was tested blind, with the CEG hidden: 91% accuracy, and every match it auto-applied was right.
notes.transition: One caveat on the R$ figure, and it works in our favor.
notes.likely_question: What is the 'expected output' percentage relative to? The model's unconstrained estimate for the same hours.

slides.title: Read R$ 8.4 bi as “at least”
columns: A new sellable product, “R$ lost per plant”, with lineage end to end (bronze → model → app) for the diligence a client runs before renewing.
Head of Data & Analytics → time-to-launch, tickets
Matching is a pipeline (CEG, fuzzy, AI; overrides win): a new product starts from one refresh run, and PT-BR questions go to Genie, not the queue.

notes.purpose: Pre-empt the 'can I trust the number' objection and show what each stakeholder takes away.
notes.talk_track: We tuned the curtailment flag for 80% precision against ONS's own flags. Recall is 41% for wind and 81% for solar, so real losses are larger than R$ 8.4 bi. We chose to under-claim rather than publish a number a client can challenge. For the Diretor Comercial, that is a sellable, defensible product that supports renewals; for the Head of Data & Analytics, a new product starts from one refresh run instead of weeks of matching, and self-service questions leave the ticket queue.
notes.transition: How is this built? One platform, six stages.
notes.likely_question: Could you raise recall? Yes, by lowering the threshold Y, at the cost of precision; it is frozen after tuning.

notes.purpose: Show the technical audience the end-to-end architecture on one platform.
notes.talk_track: Public files land through a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline into a bronze, silver, gold medallion with 17 quality expectations. Unity Catalog governs it: grants, tags, lineage, and the model itself. MLflow trains the curtailment model; ai_decide places what the rules can't. Lakebase serves five synced tables to the app, and Genie answers questions as the signed-in user, so UC grants apply per person.
notes.transition: The heart of it is the reconciliation. Here it is step by step.
notes.likely_question: Why Lakebase and not the warehouse for the app? Low latency, scale-to-zero, and the app never hits the lakehouse.

slides.title: The reconciliation, step by step
slides.body:
CEG match: normalize .01 vs .1; links the bulk of energy (910 TWh)
Complex splitting: ONS wind/solar complexes become member plants
Fuzzy name: same state and fuel; numerals must match (III never becomes II)
ai_decide: a calibrated choice among 3 candidates, or none
Human review: under 0.9 confidence goes to an in-app queue; overrides win

notes.purpose: Show the matching ladder: rules first, AI only on what remains, a human last.
notes.talk_track: CEG first, after normalizing formats; that alone links 910 TWh. Then we split ONS complexes into their member plants, measured, not guessed. Fuzzy name match next, within state and fuel, and numerals must match. What's left goes to ai_decide, which picks one of three candidates or none. Anything under 0.9 confidence lands in a review queue. Honest finding: the first AI pass said none for all 33 plants; adding name similarity, registry number and type per candidate to the prompt fixed it.
notes.transition: How was all of this built so fast?
notes.likely_question: Is the AI step repeatable? Yes: verdicts are stored once per plant and prompt, so refreshes are deterministic.

slides.subtitle: Rules first, AI only on what remains, a person last
slides.evidence_label: Honest finding: the first AI pass said “none” for all 33 plants; adding per-candidate evidence to the prompt fixed it (specs/12).

slides.title: How it was built
columns: Isaac (Claude Code) with Databricks skills; Impeccable for the frontend; code review + Isaac Review
Interview first, then 14 one-page specs with success criteria; one spec at a time
Every number traces to a committed run or executed notebook; runnable checks on each transform

notes.purpose: Explain the AI-assisted delivery approach and why it is trustworthy.
notes.talk_track: Built with Isaac, Claude Code, using the Databricks skills for pipelines, Lakebase, apps and Genie, and the Impeccable skill for the UI. Work went one small spec at a time, each with explicit success criteria, and every load-bearing decision was confirmed before implementation. Parallel read-only agents audited the git history for secrets before publishing. Every number in this deck traces to a committed run capture.
notes.transition: Building fast meant choosing. Here are the trade-offs.
notes.likely_question: How much time did AI save? Qualitatively large; we did not measure a baseline.

data: Recall 41% wind, 81% solar; R$ is a lower bound

notes.purpose: Show judgment: each choice has a stated cost and reason.
notes.talk_track: Every trade-off favors defensibility over coverage. The flag under-claims; the AI only auto-applies when it's very sure; verdicts are frozen so numbers repeat. We cut streaming and multi-tenant access control to go deep on the two hard parts: reconciliation and curtailment.
notes.transition: And none of this is a screenshot. Here is the proof.
notes.likely_question: What would production change first? Commercial PLD feed and ERA5 weather in place of Open-Meteo.

notes.purpose: Build trust by naming risks before the audience does.
notes.talk_track: Four risks, each with a mitigation already in place or a clear production path. The model estimate is reported conservatively, the AI is gated and reviewed, and the data-licensing and PLD issues have known production swaps.
notes.likely_question: What if ONS changes its file formats? Bronze ingestion is schema-tolerant, and expectations fail the refresh loudly.
